Prediction target period: from 2024-11-21 to 2024-12-09. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> The USDA released its October World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE) report on October 11, 2024, which provided updated projections for the 2023/24 and 2024/25 marketing years. For the U.S., the report indicated decreased ending stocks for corn and wheat in both marketing years. Specifically, corn ending stocks were revised down by 52 million bushels for 2023/24 and 58 million for 2024/25, while wheat stocks decreased by 6 million and 16 million bushels, respectively. Soybean ending stocks for 2023/24 saw an increase of 2 million bushels, with the 2024/25 estimate remaining unchanged. While the report lacked specific details on oats, its release influenced overall grain market sentiment, leading to an immediate decrease in corn, soybean, and wheat prices. <2> A market analysis report forecasts the global oats market will be valued at USD 4.23 billion in 2025, with North America identified as the largest market. This growth is primarily attributed to rising consumer demand for nutrient-dense and gluten-free grain options. [2] The market is further supported by U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) regulations concerning gluten-free labeling, which provide clarity for manufacturers and consumers. [2] Projections indicate the market will continue to expand, reaching USD 5.80 billion by 2030, with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 6.51%. [2] Other analyses present different valuations; one report estimated the market at USD 5.16 billion in 2023, projecting it to reach USD 8.24 billion by 2030 at a CAGR of 7.0%, and identified Europe as the largest market in 2024. [9] Another forecast suggests the market size was USD 6.73 billion in 2024 and will grow to USD 10.31 billion by 2032. [5] The increasing health consciousness among consumers, the growing popularity of plant-based diets, and the versatility of oats in various food products are key drivers across multiple analyses. [9, 4] <3> On June 28, 2024, the USDA's National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) released its Acreage report, which estimated that 2.299 million acres of oats were planted for all purposes in 2024. [1] This figure represents a decrease of nearly 10% from the 2.55 million acres that were planted in 2023. [1] The report is based on surveys conducted during the first two weeks of June 2024. [5] <4> A market analysis published on April 5, 2024, indicated that the grain sector experienced a notable price decline during the first quarter of 2024, with the grain composite falling by 7.56%. Within the sector, oats specifically decreased by 7.45% in Q1, settling at $3.57 per bushel. The report suggested that this bearish trend was extending into the start of the second quarter, as evidenced by corn futures, which fell from $4.42 per bushel on March 29, 2024, to $4.3550 by April 5, 2024. <5> A quarterly market analysis for the first quarter of 2024 reported that oat futures experienced a significant decline of 7.45%, ultimately settling at $3.57 per bushel. This decrease was consistent with a broader downward trend in the agricultural markets, as the grain composite index fell by 7.56% during the same period. <6> The USDA's National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) released its Agricultural Prices report on March 28, 2024, containing data for February 2024. The report indicated that the grain and oilseed price index fell by 6.9% from January 2024 and 28% from February 2023. Specifically, the feed grain index, which includes commodities like corn and oats, saw a decrease of 7.4% from the previous month and 35% from the prior year. The report also noted decreases in the food grain and oilseed indexes. <7> On March 28, 2024, the USDA's National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) released its annual "Prospective Plantings" report, which provides the first official, survey-based estimates of U.S. farmers' 2024 planting intentions. [3, 4, 5] The report is based on surveys conducted in the first two weeks of March with approximately 72,000 farm operators nationwide. [2, 5] It includes expected plantings for principal crops such as corn, soybeans, all wheat, and oats. [3] <8> At the North American Millers' Association (NAMA) 2024 Spring Conference, held from March 9-12 in Marco Island, Florida, Randy Strychar, president of Oatinformation, presented a comprehensive analysis of the global oat market. Strychar reported that the global trade of oats and oat products experienced a significant slowdown of 5% to 12% in nearly every region worldwide heading into 2024. This decline was particularly pronounced in the breakfast cereal and snack bar sectors, while the oat milk category remained relatively stable. Despite this slowdown, Strychar highlighted the unprecedented growth in the oat market in recent years. He also noted that global oat supplies are near record lows, with Canadian stocks being particularly tight, creating no cushion for the 2024-25 crop year. <9> The U.S. Department of Agriculture's National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) announced on February 16, 2024, that it would be conducting a nationwide survey of producers to ascertain their planting plans for the 2024 growing season. NASS planned to mail the survey questionnaires in late February. The data gathered is slated for publication in the Prospective Plantings report, which is scheduled for release on March 28, 2024. <10> The USDA released its initial 2024-25 agricultural outlook at its 100th annual Agricultural Outlook Forum held from February 15-16, 2024. The report, which influences oat prices, projected a bearish outlook for overall grain prices. For corn, the USDA forecast lower production but anticipated higher ending stocks. The outlook for soybeans included projections for lower prices and a 120 million bushel increase in ending stocks to 435 million bushels. The agency estimated farmers would plant 91 million acres of corn and 87.5 million acres of soybeans in 2024.

Prediction target period: from 2025-04-24 to 2025-05-09. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> Based on the USDA's Prospective Plantings report released on March 31, 2025, U.S. farmers signaled their intention to adjust crop acreages for the year, influenced by market conditions such as a tighter corn supply. [1, 2, 3] The report projects a 5% increase in corn planted area to 95.3 million acres, while soybean acreage is expected to decrease by 4% to 83.5 million acres. [1, 3] This shift in planting intentions for the two primary crops also affects other agricultural commodities. [2] The USDA forecasts a 2% decline in all wheat planted area to 45.4 million acres and a significant 12% drop in cotton acreage to 9.87 million acres. [2, 3] Conversely, sorghum plantings are anticipated to rise by 4%. [1] <2> The USDA's World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE) report, released on March 11, 2025, indicated minimal direct changes for the U.S. oat market but provided important context for the grain markets. The report left the U.S. corn and soybean balance sheets mostly unchanged from the prior month, with corn ending stocks holding at 1.54 billion bushels. While soybean estimates were also stable, the season-average farm price for soybeans was lowered by 15 cents to $9.95 per bushel, a move that affects the profitability and planting decisions for competing crops. A significant feature of this report was a clarifying note on trade policy, stating that the WASDE only considers tariffs in effect at the time of publication. <3> In a statement published on January 17, 2025, oat market analyst Randy Strychar predicted that the incoming U.S. presidential administration would likely implement tariffs on Canadian oats and oat products soon after the January 20 inauguration. The initial impact was expected to be felt in the feed sector, with Strychar noting that some U.S. companies were already considering halting purchases of Canadian feed oats. However, he suggested that in the longer term, U.S. millers would likely continue to import Canadian oats, pay the tariff, and ultimately pass the additional costs back to Canadian farmers. Subsequent reports in February indicated the U.S. administration signed an order for a 25% tariff on Canadian goods, set to take effect on February 4, 2025, though the implementation was later paused. <4> The USDA released its October World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE) report on October 11, 2024, which provided updated projections for the 2023/24 and 2024/25 marketing years. For the U.S., the report indicated decreased ending stocks for corn and wheat in both marketing years. Specifically, corn ending stocks were revised down by 52 million bushels for 2023/24 and 58 million for 2024/25, while wheat stocks decreased by 6 million and 16 million bushels, respectively. Soybean ending stocks for 2023/24 saw an increase of 2 million bushels, with the 2024/25 estimate remaining unchanged. While the report lacked specific details on oats, its release influenced overall grain market sentiment, leading to an immediate decrease in corn, soybean, and wheat prices. <5> A market analysis report forecasts the global oats market will be valued at USD 4.23 billion in 2025, with North America identified as the largest market. This growth is primarily attributed to rising consumer demand for nutrient-dense and gluten-free grain options. [2] The market is further supported by U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) regulations concerning gluten-free labeling, which provide clarity for manufacturers and consumers. [2] Projections indicate the market will continue to expand, reaching USD 5.80 billion by 2030, with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 6.51%. [2] Other analyses present different valuations; one report estimated the market at USD 5.16 billion in 2023, projecting it to reach USD 8.24 billion by 2030 at a CAGR of 7.0%, and identified Europe as the largest market in 2024. [9] Another forecast suggests the market size was USD 6.73 billion in 2024 and will grow to USD 10.31 billion by 2032. [5] The increasing health consciousness among consumers, the growing popularity of plant-based diets, and the versatility of oats in various food products are key drivers across multiple analyses. [9, 4] <6> On June 28, 2024, the USDA's National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) released its Acreage report, which estimated that 2.299 million acres of oats were planted for all purposes in 2024. [1] This figure represents a decrease of nearly 10% from the 2.55 million acres that were planted in 2023. [1] The report is based on surveys conducted during the first two weeks of June 2024. [5] <7> A market analysis published on April 5, 2024, indicated that the grain sector experienced a notable price decline during the first quarter of 2024, with the grain composite falling by 7.56%. Within the sector, oats specifically decreased by 7.45% in Q1, settling at $3.57 per bushel. The report suggested that this bearish trend was extending into the start of the second quarter, as evidenced by corn futures, which fell from $4.42 per bushel on March 29, 2024, to $4.3550 by April 5, 2024. <8> A quarterly market analysis for the first quarter of 2024 reported that oat futures experienced a significant decline of 7.45%, ultimately settling at $3.57 per bushel. This decrease was consistent with a broader downward trend in the agricultural markets, as the grain composite index fell by 7.56% during the same period. <9> The USDA's National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) released its Agricultural Prices report on March 28, 2024, containing data for February 2024. The report indicated that the grain and oilseed price index fell by 6.9% from January 2024 and 28% from February 2023. Specifically, the feed grain index, which includes commodities like corn and oats, saw a decrease of 7.4% from the previous month and 35% from the prior year. The report also noted decreases in the food grain and oilseed indexes. <10> On March 28, 2024, the USDA's National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) released its annual "Prospective Plantings" report, which provides the first official, survey-based estimates of U.S. farmers' 2024 planting intentions. [3, 4, 5] The report is based on surveys conducted in the first two weeks of March with approximately 72,000 farm operators nationwide. [2, 5] It includes expected plantings for principal crops such as corn, soybeans, all wheat, and oats. [3]

[2, 3] This surge was driven by importers front-loading shipments to get ahead of potential tariff changes. [2, 3] The activity resulted in a record-breaking month for the Port of Los Angeles, which handled over 1.01 million TEUs, its highest monthly total ever. [3, 5] The Port of Long Beach also saw its third-busiest month, processing 944,232 TEUs. [3, 6] This spike in volume placed considerable pressure on local fleets and the broader inland transportation network, increasing logistics costs and exacerbating port congestion. [4] While the influx tested the system, port fluidity remained stable, with truck and rail dwell times not seeing a significant negative impact due to effective coordination between supply chain partners. [4] However, officials anticipate that this surge may be temporary, with forecasts suggesting a potential decline in cargo volumes in the latter half of the year as the front-loaded inventory is absorbed and the impact of trade policies is realized. [2, 6] <2> A freight market update for July 2025 indicates that U.S. ground transportation is facing significant capacity constraints. This pressure is driven by a combination of a U.S. truck driver shortage amounting to 80,000 drivers and increasing costs from rising port tariffs. Furthermore, demand for trucking and rail has returned to pre-pandemic levels, while rerouted ocean freight is also contributing to higher overall freight rates. <3> A market trends report from Grain Farmers of Ontario identified the July 4th, 2025, weekend as a crucial time for market price direction. The report highlighted that increasing summer heat across the U.S. corn belt could significantly impact what has been, up to that point, a very good crop. This market analysis was published following the USDA's annual Acreage report, which was released on June 30, 2025, providing the first official survey-based estimates of planted acreage for the year. [2, 3, 4, 6] <4> Based on the USDA's Prospective Plantings report released on March 31, 2025, U.S. farmers signaled their intention to adjust crop acreages for the year, influenced by market conditions such as a tighter corn supply. [1, 2, 3] The report projects a 5% increase in corn planted area to 95.3 million acres, while soybean acreage is expected to decrease by 4% to 83.5 million acres. [1, 3] This shift in planting intentions for the two primary crops also affects other agricultural commodities. [2] The USDA forecasts a 2% decline in all wheat planted area to 45.4 million acres and a significant 12% drop in cotton acreage to 9.87 million acres. [2, 3] Conversely, sorghum plantings are anticipated to rise by 4%. [1] <5> The USDA's World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE) report, released on March 11, 2025, indicated minimal direct changes for the U.S. oat market but provided important context for the grain markets. The report left the U.S. corn and soybean balance sheets mostly unchanged from the prior month, with corn ending stocks holding at 1.54 billion bushels. While soybean estimates were also stable, the season-average farm price for soybeans was lowered by 15 cents to $9.95 per bushel, a move that affects the profitability and planting decisions for competing crops. A significant feature of this report was a clarifying note on trade policy, stating that the WASDE only considers tariffs in effect at the time of publication. <6> In a statement published on January 17, 2025, oat market analyst Randy Strychar predicted that the incoming U.S. presidential administration would likely implement tariffs on Canadian oats and oat products soon after the January 20 inauguration. The initial impact was expected to be felt in the feed sector, with Strychar noting that some U.S. companies were already considering halting purchases of Canadian feed oats. However, he suggested that in the longer term, U.S. millers would likely continue to import Canadian oats, pay the tariff, and ultimately pass the additional costs back to Canadian farmers. Subsequent reports in February indicated the U.S. administration signed an order for a 25% tariff on Canadian goods, set to take effect on February 4, 2025, though the implementation was later paused. <7> The USDA released its October World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE) report on October 11, 2024, which provided updated projections for the 2023/24 and 2024/25 marketing years. For the U.S., the report indicated decreased ending stocks for corn and wheat in both marketing years. Specifically, corn ending stocks were revised down by 52 million bushels for 2023/24 and 58 million for 2024/25, while wheat stocks decreased by 6 million and 16 million bushels, respectively. Soybean ending stocks for 2023/24 saw an increase of 2 million bushels, with the 2024/25 estimate remaining unchanged. While the report lacked specific details on oats, its release influenced overall grain market sentiment, leading to an immediate decrease in corn, soybean, and wheat prices. <8> A market analysis report forecasts the global oats market will be valued at USD 4.23 billion in 2025, with North America identified as the largest market. This growth is primarily attributed to rising consumer demand for nutrient-dense and gluten-free grain options. [2] The market is further supported by U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) regulations concerning gluten-free labeling, which provide clarity for manufacturers and consumers. [2] Projections indicate the market will continue to expand, reaching USD 5.80 billion by 2030, with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 6.51%. [2] Other analyses present different valuations; one report estimated the market at USD 5.16 billion in 2023, projecting it to reach USD 8.24 billion by 2030 at a CAGR of 7.0%, and identified Europe as the largest market in 2024. [9] Another forecast suggests the market size was USD 6.73 billion in 2024 and will grow to USD 10.31 billion by 2032. [5] The increasing health consciousness among consumers, the growing popularity of plant-based diets, and the versatility of oats in various food products are key drivers across multiple analyses. [9, 4] <9> On June 28, 2024, the USDA's National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) released its Acreage report, which estimated that 2.299 million acres of oats were planted for all purposes in 2024. [1] This figure represents a decrease of nearly 10% from the 2.55 million acres that were planted in 2023. [1] The report is based on surveys conducted during the first two weeks of June 2024. [5] <10> A market analysis published on April 5, 2024, indicated that the grain sector experienced a notable price decline during the first quarter of 2024, with the grain composite falling by 7.56%. Within the sector, oats specifically decreased by 7.45% in Q1, settling at $3.57 per bushel. The report suggested that this bearish trend was extending into the start of the second quarter, as evidenced by corn futures, which fell from $4.42 per bushel on March 29, 2024, to $4.3550 by April 5, 2024.
